defaults.permitted_development: Across Bedfordshire, a modest roof-light on a house is usually permitted development if it projects no more than 150mm from the existing roof slope, does not exceed the height of the existing roof and the property still benefits from normal householder rights. Planning permission becomes more likely where the work is on a listed building, in a controlled area or tied to a wider roof enlargement.

rules.height_rules: Across Bedfordshire, a roof-light must not push the roof above the existing highest part. Keeping the frame low-profile and subordinate to the roof slope is usually the safest approach.
rules.depth_rules: Across Bedfordshire, the unit must not project more than 150 millimetres from the plane of the existing roof slope. Once the projection starts to read as a box, dormer or raised roof feature, the simpler roof-light route usually stops applying.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Bedfordshire, boundary impact usually comes through privacy rather than distance. Side-facing roof-light windows should be obscure-glazed and, if openable, the opening part should have its lowest point at least 1.7 metres above the room floor.
rules.roof_rules: Across Bedfordshire, the proposal should read as a modest alteration to the existing roof rather than a new roof form in its own right. Roof terraces and larger enlargements are separate development types with stricter rules.
rules.materials_rules: Across Bedfordshire, choose a roof-light that feels recessive rather than attention-seeking. Simple frame colours, tidy flashings and detailing that works with the existing roof covering generally give the strongest planning outcome.

restrictions.conservation_area: Roof-lights on prominent roof slopes in conservation areas often face a closer design review, especially where they would affect a traditional roofscape or visible frontage.
restrictions.listed_building: Roof-lights in listed buildings are commonly treated as heritage works because the roof covering, structure and external appearance all contribute to significance.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions or roof-specific planning conditions can remove the usual householder right to add roof-lights, especially on visible elevations or in heritage areas.

rules.permitted_development: For houses in Central Bedfordshire, the usual roof-light route is to keep the unit modest: no more than 150mm projection from the existing roof slope and no increase above the existing roof height. Once the proposal sits on a more sensitive roofscape or forms part of a larger roof alteration, planning permission is more likely to be needed.

rules.height_rules: Height control for a roof-light is simple but strict: the proposal should not rise above the existing roof. The more flush and subordinate the unit appears, the easier the scheme is to keep within the normal householder route.
rules.depth_rules: The unit must not project more than 150 millimetres from the plane of the existing roof slope. Once the projection starts to read as a box, dormer or raised roof feature, the simpler roof-light route usually stops applying.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary impact usually comes through privacy rather than distance. Side-facing roof-light windows should be obscure-glazed and, if openable, the opening part should have its lowest point at least 1.7 metres above the room floor.
rules.roof_rules: The proposal should read as a modest alteration to the existing roof rather than a new roof form in its own right. Roof terraces and larger enlargements are separate development types with stricter rules.
rules.materials_rules: Materials are not just about weathering: they control how visible the roof-light looks. Neat flashings, restrained frame colours and a low-profile unit usually sit better than bright trims or bulky cassettes.

restrictions.conservation_area: In conservation areas, even small roof-lights can need closer scrutiny if they are proposed on prominent slopes or on buildings with a consistent historic roofscape.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed building consent may be required for roof-lights where the work alters historic roof fabric, framing, coverings or the character of the building.
restrictions.article4_notes: Do not assume the standard roof-light allowance survives everywhere: Article 4 controls and site-specific conditions can require an application for visible roof changes.

rules.permitted_development: For houses in Luton, the usual roof-light route is to keep the unit modest: no more than 150mm projection from the existing roof slope and no increase above the existing roof height. Once the proposal sits on a more sensitive roofscape or forms part of a larger roof alteration, planning permission is more likely to be needed.

rules.height_rules: The alteration must not exceed the height of the existing roof. In practice that means choosing a low-profile unit that sits quietly within the roof slope rather than reading as an added structure on top of it.
rules.depth_rules: Depth is controlled by projection from the roof plane rather than by the size of the opening alone. Once the unit projects more than 150mm, the straightforward householder route is usually lost.
rules.boundary_rules: Roof-lights do not have a normal setback rule, but side-facing windows can still affect neighbours. Obscure glazing and a 1.7 metre minimum level to any opening part are the usual privacy conditions.
rules.roof_rules: The proposal should read as a modest alteration to the existing roof rather than a new roof form in its own right. Roof terraces and larger enlargements are separate development types with stricter rules.
rules.materials_rules: Choose a roof-light that feels recessive rather than attention-seeking. Simple frame colours, tidy flashings and detailing that works with the existing roof covering generally give the strongest planning outcome.

restrictions.conservation_area: A roof-light in a conservation area is usually easiest to justify when it is discreetly placed and does not disrupt an established roof form.
